hypothesis: The classic three-way tension between dispatch gas, expressiveness, and verifiability is not fundamental but an artifact of hand-written assembly interpreters: a Weiroll-class chaining VM can be simultaneously near-gas-optimal AND carry a machine-checked correctness certificate by splitting concerns into (a) a formally-specified IR/semantics layer used only to PROVE a script offchain (IELE/KEVM/Yul-semantics style), and (b) an onchain dispatch loop whose memory-copy and stack sequences are emitted or validated by an EVM superoptimizer (Max-SMT/GASOL lineage) and certified by verified block-optimization. Under this split, verification migrates off the hot path; the assembly interpreter is treated as compiled, machine-checked output rather than something proven line-by-line, refuting the assumption that gas-tuned assembly dispatch forecloses formal verifiability.
rationale: IELE was designed expressly with formal semantics to ease verification, and KEVM plus an operational semantics for Yul show a script's high-level meaning can live in a checkable IR even when the deployed artifact is opaque assembly. The Max-SMT superoptimizer family (A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage; GASOL; Synthesis of Super-Optimized Smart Contracts Using Max-SMT) demonstrates constraint solvers can emit provably gas-minimal bytecode for a fixed semantics, and Formally Verified EVM Block-Optimizations plus Secure Optimizations on Ethereum Bytecode Jump-Free Sequences show such optimizations can themselves be certified. Inferring Needless Write Memory Accesses on Ethereum Bytecode confirms the memory-copy layer (the exact mcopy-style chaining region in this codebase) is a tractable optimization target. Together these post-Weiroll, low-citation works imply the 'verifiable vs gas-optimal' gap is bridgeable by construction, with MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum as the concrete dispatch-layer artifact to which this applies.
supports_if: A chaining/multicall interpreter is shown to (a) compile scripts from a formally-specified IR (IELE/KEVM/Yul-semantics checkable), (b) have its memory-copy/dispatch sequences emitted or validated by a Max-SMT/GASOL-class superoptimizer such that per-call dispatch gas matches or beats a hand-tuned assembly baseline, and (c) ship a mechanized proof (block-optimization-certified) that decode+dispatch preserves the IR semantics — with measured gas within a few percent of the unverified baseline.
refutes_if: Adding an IELE/KEVM-style verifiable IR or a superoptimizer/certified-optimization pass is measured to impose a persistent, non-trivial onchain dispatch-gas penalty that cannot be eliminated (e.g. register-machine or proof-carrying overhead), OR the assembly interpreter cannot be derived from / checked against the IR without re-introducing manual line-by-line verification — i.e. gas-optimality and machine-checked verifiability remain empirically mutually exclusive for the dispatch layer.
motivating_papers: IELE: An Intermediate-Level Blockchain Language Designed and Implemented Using Formal Semantics
KEVM: A Complete Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine
A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage
GASOL: Gas Analysis and Optimization for Ethereum Smart Contracts
Synthesis of Super-Optimized Smart Contracts Using Max-SMT
Secure Optimizations on Ethereum Bytecode Jump-Free Sequences
Inferring Needless Write Memory Accesses on Ethereum Bytecode
MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum

hypothesis: Composability for a chaining multicall VM should be specified and verified not as type-safe return-data plumbing but as an MEV non-interference property: a script is 'safely composable' iff the value chained from call i into call j is non-interferent with adversarially insertable state between those sub-calls. This reframing predicts the most consequential correctness/security defects in Weiroll-class interpreters are not memory-offset-encoding bugs but value-substitution attacks on a chained intermediate result (e.g. a quote/balance an inserted action can move), and that the right verifiable design bakes a per-edge freshness/atomicity guarantee into the offset descriptor itself rather than only proving byte-copy correctness.
rationale: DeFi Composability as MEV Non-interference recasts composability as an information-flow/non-interference question, arriving after Weiroll's design and so unavailable to it; Formal Analysis of Composable DeFi Protocols and Towards Verified Price Oracles for Decentralized Exchange Protocols supply the formal machinery for reasoning about composed/oracle-dependent flows, and Know Your Intent: An Autonomous Multi-Perspective LLM Agent Framework for DeFi User Transaction Intent Mining marks the shift to intents as the unit of composition. A chaining VM's defining feature is exactly that a return value crosses a trust boundary between sub-calls, which is precisely what non-interference formalizes; this predicts descriptors should carry a verifiable atomicity/freshness check, making the security-relevant property checkable rather than implicit in the current memTarget/resultLength encoding.
supports_if: A non-interference / information-flow specification applied to a chaining VM detects real chained-value manipulation vulnerabilities that pure offset-encoding/memory-safety verification misses, AND an interpreter design embedding a per-edge atomicity/freshness check in the chaining descriptor demonstrably blocks them at modest gas cost.
refutes_if: Empirical analysis of chaining-VM failures shows defects are dominated by memory-layout/offset-encoding mistakes with no distinct, exploitable class explained only by MEV non-interference, OR a non-interference specification yields no detection or design guidance beyond what memory-safety plus atomic-execution proofs already provide.
motivating_papers: Formal Analysis of Composable DeFi Protocols
Towards Verified Price Oracles for Decentralized Exchange Protocols
Know Your Intent: An Autonomous Multi-Perspective LLM Agent Framework for DeFi User Transaction Intent Mining
MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum
